name: Ivan Larsen

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: I am with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI firms, employers, unions or government. We sell nothing and campaign for no side. Your answers are confidential. Tell me about a normal workday.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I teach beginner French horn on Tuesdays, play junior horn parts in the local orchestra and arrange simple school pieces when asked. I finished secondary school and still watch the lead horn player on a difficult entrance.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What keeps you at it, and what wears on you?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I like a pupil getting the first clean note. I do not like accepting an orchestra date and then seeing the family pickup plan change the next morning.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AI Plateau. "Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway."

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would tell the local orchestra that a quicker booking sheet is fine, but a player still has to turn up and read the part. I would keep my Tuesday brass lessons and weekend concerts.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: We have eleven months of expenses saved, and my partner’s teaching wage is steady. I am still the junior horn player, but one lost concert fee would not disturb the mortgage.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I will keep teaching beginner French horn on Tuesdays and taking the orchestra calls this year. I would ask the contractor for the autumn dates before buying a new mouthpiece.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel calm about our bills. We have earned a cushion, and I do not need a new tool to know when a student is short of breath.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What happened when the concert moved rooms?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The last concert moved to a smaller room and still paid the contracted fee. I would ask for the same cancellation terms next season before promising money for a family holiday.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What does your son see when you practise?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My son watches me practise the high passage until I can play it without a crack. That is a better lesson about work than a perfect recording on a screen.

say: I would tell players that **booking sheets** may improve while live parts still need us.
I would keep the **contracted concert fee** for room changes.
think: Our **eleven-month cushion** and partner’s teaching pay secure the mortgage.
I still watch **orchestra calls** because I am a junior player.
do: Keep **Tuesday horn pupils** and weekend concerts this year.
Ask the contractor for **autumn dates** before buying a mouthpiece.
feel: I feel **calm** because the household can absorb one missed concert.
S0.quote: My son watches me practise the high passage until I can play it without a crack.
fieldNote: His **eleven-month reserve** and steady partner teaching wage explain his calm reaction to an ordinary lost concert.
He uses **no AI tools** and treats repeated practice as his teaching method.

steps.text: Keep Tuesday horn pupils and weekend orchestra concerts
Wait for autumn concert dates before buying a new mouthpiece

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Steady Disruption. "Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust."

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would tell the contractor that AI might book shows, write parts and choose background music, and players need a written paid schedule. I would ask our musicians association to check the rehearsal minimum.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The simple horn arrangements I make for school shows may lose buyers. Our savings mean the mortgage is safe, but losing my own fee still matters and the orchestra may shorten rehearsals.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Next month I would bring the last two paid schedules to the association and ask the contractor for the next one. In the first year I would keep my Tuesday pupils and ask two nearby orchestras about advertised paid seats only if my calls actually fall.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would be anxious about losing arranging money and possibly paid rehearsals. Eleven months of savings do not put paid rehearsals on the contractor’s calendar.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you apply for any nearby orchestra seat?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would not audition for a seat whose part I cannot yet play. I would ask the lead horn player to hear me first and apply only when I can manage the excerpts and school pickup.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What should the association compare?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The association needs to put the number of paid rehearsals beside last year’s number. I will not argue from a rumour about a computer.

say: I would ask for a **written paid schedule** before software changes bookings.
I would bring the **association** into rehearsal-hour decisions.
think: My **school arrangements** may lose buyers as AI writes parts.
Paid **rehearsal hours** may shrink even while the mortgage stays safe.
do: Bring two **paid schedules** to the association next month.
Ask about **advertised orchestra seats** only if calls fall, excerpts are ready and pickup fits.
feel: I feel **anxious** about my own fees and possible rehearsal cuts.
S1.quote: Eleven months of savings do not put paid rehearsals on the contractor’s calendar.
fieldNote: His personal **arrangement income** is exposed despite strong household reserves.
The job option needs an **advertised paid seat**, ready excerpts and pickup fit, not just nearby posts.

steps.text: Bring two paid schedules to musicians association for rehearsal comparison

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2028. "Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare."

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would tell the orchestra that AGI by 2028 could make the school arrangements cheaply, but the players must be paid for rehearsal. I would ask the contractor for the season schedule in writing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I expect my arrangement fees to end in 2028, and the contractor might pay for fewer rehearsals then. Robots that play hands-on parts arrive around 2031, so the horn seat lasts longer, but I cannot assume it is safe forever.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: This week I would take my arrangement invoices to the association and ask the contractor for signed autumn dates. If 2028 AGI reduces paid calls, I would audition for an advertised paid horn seat only after the lead player says my excerpts are ready and the hours fit child pickup; I would keep pupils until a contract is signed.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would be anxious about losing arrangements and perhaps some paid calls. Eleven months saved gives me time to audition, but it does not replace my school arrangement fees.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How much savings would you protect while auditioning?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would keep six months of expenses untouched during auditions. If the only opening needs a qualification I do not have, I would not treat it as an option.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell the family?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would tell my partner the score fees are likely gone, but the orchestra chair is still ours for now. I would not ask our children to change schools because of an unsigned audition.

say: I would demand **signed autumn dates** before trusting the next season.
I would argue for **paid horn rehearsals** while the seat exists.
think: My **arrangement fees** likely end in 2028 before 2031 playing robots.
The contractor could cut **paid calls** before any robot appears.
do: Take **arrangement invoices** to the association this week.
Audition for an **advertised paid horn seat** after 2028 cuts only with ready excerpts, qualifications and pickup fit.
Keep **horn pupils** until signed offer, leaving six months of savings untouched during auditions.
feel: I feel **anxious** about my own lost fees, with time to search.
S2.quote: Eleven months saved gives me time to audition, but it does not replace my school arrangement fees.
fieldNote: He separates **2028 score loss** from later 2031 robot performance.
His next seat needs **signed paid work** and ready excerpts, qualification and pickup fit, with a six-month reserve.

steps.text: Take arrangement invoices to association before season decision
Audition for advertised paid horn seat if 2028 calls fall, qualified, excerpts ready and pickup fits

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2031. "Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast."

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would tell my children that AGI by 2031 gives us years to learn a trade well. I would ask the orchestra to pay a senior player to train the next horn player, not expect unpaid shadows.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I think the school arrangements will vanish by 2031, but I could add dependable horn pupils by then. Robots around 2034 may play onstage, though I do not know if a conductor would trust one.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: This autumn I would ask the orchestra for a paid observation hour with the lead horn player if it fits child pickup. If the contractor funds it, I would practise the hard excerpts under supervision; in the first year after 2031 I would keep teaching paid pupils and audition only for seats I can play.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would be anxious about lost arranging pay until pupils replace it. Practising horn excerpts does not guarantee me a paid orchestra seat.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who should be paid for the observation?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The senior player should be paid for that hour, and I would not call an unpaid rehearsal a lesson. I need to improve, but I cannot take work away from the family for nothing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What if your excerpts are still weak?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would ask the lead player for a blunt assessment. If my excerpts are still weak, I would stay with my present chair and keep practising.

say: I would seek a **paid senior observation** for my horn playing.
I would tell my children that **practice time** has a purpose.
think: My **school arrangements** may end by 2031 before 2034 stage robots.
More **paid pupils** might replace the lost fees if bookings grow.
do: Ask for a **funded senior observation** this autumn only if child pickup fits.
Keep **paid horn pupils** after 2031 and audition only for seats I can play.
feel: I feel **anxious** until lessons replace lost arrangement pay.
S3.quote: Practising horn excerpts does not guarantee me a paid orchestra seat.
fieldNote: He requires **funded senior time** and pickup fit before the observation.
His job move waits for **honest excerpt readiness**, not a title or hopeful audition.

steps.text: Practise horn excerpts with lead player only if contractor funds observation and pickup fits
Keep paid horn pupils after 2031 while families book
Audition for suitable horn seats after 2031 only if excerpts are ready

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2036. "Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans."

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would tell my children that AGI by 2036 leaves time to learn the horn and useful work beyond it. I would keep playing paid concerts while the contractor books us.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: By 2036 I might have enough pupils to live without arrangements. Robots around 2039 may play horn parts, but the current orchestra pay and our savings make the next few years secure.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Starting this year I would save half of each paid arrangement fee until our reserve reaches twelve months. In the first year after 2036 I would compare signed concert calls with last year and audition for a qualified advertised local seat only if calls fall, my excerpts are ready and school pickup fits.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would feel uneasy about possible stage work later. Our mortgage is covered now, and I have years to teach more pupils.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is the twelve-month target already saved?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Twelve months is a target, not what we have today. If arrangements stop early, I would keep six months untouched and save from lessons only after the family bills are paid.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you teach your children about work?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would tell my children to learn their craft before they promise a fee. Skill and a reliable contract travel farther than a shiny tool.

say: I would tell children to **learn a craft** before charging for it.
I would keep **paid concerts** while the contractor books players.
think: More **horn pupils** could replace arrangements before 2036.
Possible **2039 stage robots** do not disturb next year’s signed work.
do: Save half of **paid arrangement fees**; if they stop, save spare lesson fees after bills, keeping six months untouched.
Audition for an **advertised paid seat** after 2036 only if calls fall, qualifications and excerpts fit, and pickup works.
Keep **paid orchestra concerts** while the contractor continues booking players.
feel: I feel **uneasy** about distant stage work while current bills are covered.
S4.quote: Skill and a reliable contract travel farther than a shiny tool.
fieldNote: His reserve target is **twelve months**, built from paid work while protecting six months if arrangements stop.
His later audition needs **paid posted work**, qualification, excerpt readiness and pickup fit.

steps.text: Save half of paid arrangement fees toward twelve months while fees continue

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028 worries me most because arrangement fees may go before the orchestra signs its season. A written paid schedule, a funded senior observation and a suitable advertised horn post would help.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Ask who pays the senior player for teaching the next one. A young horn player cannot learn by watching an empty chair.

headlineQuote: A young horn player cannot learn by watching an empty chair.
portrait: At **43**, Ivan is a junior horn player with secondary school education, two children, a mortgage and eleven months saved.
His partner’s **teaching wage** and many nearby posts give options despite exposed arrangement fees.
He avoids **AI tools** and relies on handwritten practice, paid senior observation and ready excerpts.
Across AGI dates, he protects **six months** of savings and auditions only for qualified paid seats fitting school pickup.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028** may erase arrangement fees before the orchestra signs its next paid season.
whatWouldHelp: A **written schedule**, funded senior observation and suitable advertised horn post would help Ivan keep earning.
